group.passage:
On a June morning in 1974, a cashier at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, passed a pack of chewing gum over a scanner, and a machine read the striped label printed on it. It was the first time a store had rung up a product by reading its Universal Product Code. The idea behind that beep, however, was already more than twenty years old.
In the late 1940s, the head of a grocery chain asked Drexel University in Philadelphia for help finding a faster way to record items at the checkout. Two graduate students, Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver, took up the challenge. Woodland, who had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, later said he had simply stretched its dots and dashes downward into narrow and wide lines. Their patent, filed in 1949 and granted in 1952, arranged the lines in rings like a bull's-eye, so that the code could be read from any direction.
Yet the invention arrived too early. Reliable scanners did not exist, and it took years for laser technology to catch up. Many grocers also resisted a single system for the whole industry, and food companies disliked the idea of paying to print a code on every package.
The breakthrough came in the early 1970s at IBM. An engineer named George Laurer was asked to write a proposal explaining how the bull's-eye code could be made to work in supermarkets. Instead, he returned with a design of his own. The round code, he had concluded, was too small and would smear on the cheap printing presses used for most food labels, so he replaced the rings with straight rows of bars. In 1973 the grocery industry adopted his design as its standard, and Woodland himself joined the team that refined it.
What followed surprised even Laurer. IBM never patented the code; it let anyone use it and sold the machines needed to read it. Between 1976 and 1980, the number of stores using the system jumped from 104 to 2,207. Laurer had expected his invention to be replaced within a decade or so. Today, barcodes are scanned more than six billion times a day.

questions.stem: Which of the following questions does the passage answer?

options.A: Why did Laurer give up on the round design?
options.B: How much did the first scanned pack of gum cost?
options.C: Which company built the scanner used in Troy, Ohio?
options.D: When did stores in Europe begin to use barcodes?

questions.stem: Why did IBM most likely choose not to patent the code?

options.A: Woodland and Silver still owned the rights to the code.
options.B: Laurer asked the company to give his new design away for free.
options.C: The design was too simple to be protected by law.
options.D: Free use of the code would boost sales of its scanners.

questions.stem: According to the passage, about how many times as many stores used the system in 1980 as in 1976?

options.D: About two hundred times as many.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that Laurer expected his invention to be replaced within a decade or so?

options.A: To show that its success went far beyond expectations.
options.B: To explain why IBM decided not to patent the code.
options.C: To suggest that barcodes will soon be out of date.
options.D: To show that Laurer had little faith in his own design.

evidence: IBM never patented the code; it let anyone use it and sold the machines needed to read it.

hints: 找出 1976 年和 1980 年的商店數。

4.explanation_zh: 第五段一開頭說「接下來的發展連勞爾都感到意外」；他原以為條碼大約十年內就會被取代，結果今天每天被掃描超過六十億次。作者提到他的預期，是為了凸顯條碼的成功遠超出設計者本人的想像。
evidence: Laurer had expected his invention to be replaced within a decade or so.

option_notes_zh.B: 相鄰句誤連：IBM 不申請專利、出售讀取機器是另一件事，文中沒有把它和勞爾的預期連在一起。
option_notes_zh.C: 與原文相反：下一句說條碼至今每天仍被掃描六十億次以上。
option_notes_zh.D: 過度解讀：勞爾違背主管指示，提出自己的設計，可見他相信這個設計；這句話的重點是成功超出預期，不是他不信任設計。

B: IBM never patented the code; it let anyone use it and sold the machines needed to read it.
C: Today, barcodes are scanned more than six billion times a day.
D: Instead, he returned with a design of his own.

4.strategy_zh: 目的題把這句話放回段落：段首句（surprised even Laurer）和後一句（今天每天六十億次）形成對比，作者用「預期」襯托「實際」。
hints: 第五段第一句說什麼事讓勞爾意外？
勞爾原本的預期和今天的情況有什麼差別？
作者用這個對比想強調什麼？

translation_zh.text:
1974 年 6 月的一個早晨，美國俄亥俄州特洛伊市一家超市的收銀員把一包口香糖從掃描器上方滑過，機器讀出了印在包裝上的條紋標籤。這是商店第一次以讀取「通用產品碼」的方式結帳。不過，那一聲「嗶」背後的構想，當時已經有二十多年的歷史。
1940 年代末，一家連鎖雜貨店的負責人請費城的德雷塞爾大學幫忙，想找出在結帳時更快登錄商品的方法。兩名研究生諾曼・約瑟夫・伍德蘭和伯納德・席佛接下了這個挑戰。伍德蘭當童子軍時學過摩斯電碼，他後來說，自己只是把摩斯電碼的點和劃往下拉長，變成窄線和寬線。他們的專利在 1949 年提出申請、1952 年獲准，把線條排成像靶心一樣的圓環，讓條碼從任何方向都能讀取。
然而這項發明出現得太早了。當時沒有可靠的掃描器，雷射技術過了好多年才趕上。許多雜貨商也抗拒全業界使用單一系統，食品公司則不願意花錢在每個包裝上印條碼。
突破出現在 1970 年代初的 IBM。一位名叫喬治・勞爾的工程師奉命寫一份提案，說明如何讓牛眼條碼在超市中派上用場。結果他交回的是自己的設計。他判斷圓形條碼太小，在大多數食品標籤使用的廉價印刷機上會暈開，於是把圓環換成一排排直條。1973 年，雜貨業採用他的設計作為標準，伍德蘭本人也加入團隊協助改良。
接下來的發展連勞爾都感到意外。IBM 從未為這套條碼申請專利；它讓任何人都能使用，並出售讀取條碼所需的機器。1976 到 1980 年間，使用這套系統的商店從 104 家暴增到 2,207 家。勞爾原本預期他的發明大約十年內就會被取代。如今，條碼每天被掃描超過六十億次。

open_tasks.prompt: IBM chose to let anyone use the barcode for free. Do you think giving away an invention can be a smart business decision? Answer in 1–2 English sentences and use an example from the passage.
reference_answers: Yes, because when IBM let everyone use the barcode, more stores adopted it and needed IBM's scanners, so the free code helped IBM sell more machines.
It can be, but only if the company sells something else that people need, like the scanners IBM sold to read the free code.
